information_for_contributors: Graphviz / DOT. Small language, published grammar, so this one can afford
to be fairly literal about it — see the DOT language definition at
https://graphviz.org/doc/info/lang.html.
Three decisions carry their reasons here.
1. `<` always opens an HTML-like label. DOT has no comparison operators and
no generics, so outside a quoted string the only thing an angle bracket
can be is the start of `label=<bold>`. That is why the rule needs
no `(?<==)` guard, which is fortunate: Oniguruma would not take a
variable-length one. Inside the label the built-in HTML grammar is
included, and it is what makes the naive `<` … `>` pair work at all —
HTML consumes `<b>` including its `>`, so the end pattern is only
reached at the `>` that closes the label. The known cost is a bare
greater-than in label text (`<a > b>`), which ends the label early.
2. `#` is a comment only at the start of a line, because that is all DOT
promises: a `#` line is C-preprocessor output. The md renderer's
`isRawGraphviz` refuses to skip those lines for a related reason — every
Markdown heading also starts with `#`, so a `.gv` file that opens with a
comment is rendered as Markdown (port spec §5, rule 69). Nothing here
can fix that; it is recorded so the two behaviours are not read as a
contradiction.
3. Identifiers accept letters, marks and numbers rather than plain `\w`.
Rule 70 of the port spec is the story: a name in NFD such as
`digraph café {` ended early when the name run did not accept combining
marks, and the file then rendered as Markdown on VS Code alone.
There is deliberately no `$schema` key: it makes VS Code fetch a schema
over the network when this file is opened.
The scope name must stay `source.graphviz` — package.json's `grammars`
entry and the fenced-block injection both name it.
name: Graphviz

patterns.comment: See note 2 in the header: only at the start of a line.

graph-header.comment: `strict digraph Name {`. The name is optional and may also be a quoted string, in which case capture 3 does not match, the rule stops after the keyword, and the string rule picks it up.

subgraph-header.comment: `subgraph cluster_a {`. Kept separate from the graph header only because `strict` may not precede it.

default-attribute-statement.comment: `node [shape=box]` / `edge [color=grey]`. The lookahead is what distinguishes the keyword from a node called `node`, which DOT allows and people write.
default-attribute-statement.name: storage.type.graphviz

html-label.comment: See note 1 in the header. `text.html.basic` comes from VS Code's built-in HTML extension, which the author is allowed to disable — and a missing include that is a rule's ONLY pattern takes the rule down with it, measured against vscode-textmate 9 with real Oniguruma. Without the sibling below, disabling HTML would leave `label=<hi>` with no scopes at all, not merely without HTML ones. When HTML is present it wins every tie, because an include contributes its patterns ahead of what follows it.

html-label-minimal.comment: The floor for the HTML label. It matches a whole tag, closing angle bracket included, and that is the point: the `<` … `>` pair above relies on its inner patterns to eat the `>` of every nested tag, so a fallback that stopped at the tag name would end the label at the first `<b>` and spill the rest of the label into the graph.

strings.comment: DOT strings may span lines — a trailing backslash is the documented line continuation — so this is genuinely multi-line and not clipped at the end of the line the way PlantUML's is.
strings.name: string.quoted.double.graphviz

patterns.comment: `\"`, `\\`, the line continuation, and the label escapes `\N` `\G` `\E` `\T` `\H` `\L` `\l` `\r`.
patterns.name: constant.character.escape.graphviz

edge-operator.comment: `->` in a digraph, `--` in a graph. Mixing them is an error Graphviz reports; the grammar does not try to, because it has no idea which kind of graph it is in.
edge-operator.name: keyword.operator.edge.graphviz

attribute.comment: `shape=box`, and the bare `rankdir=LR;` form that sits at graph level outside any bracket — which is why this rule is not confined to `#attribute-list`.
